title: Weakly Supervised Polar Low Segmentation in Sentinel-1 SAR Imagery

paper.title: Weakly Supervised Polar Low Segmentation in Sentinel-1 SAR Imagery
paper.abstract:
Abstract Polar lows are intense maritime cyclones that form rapidly at high latitudes.
Deep learning can detect them in Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, but pixel-level segmentation remains an open challenge.
No pixel-level masks are available for training, and a polar low’s extent is inherently subjective, with diffuse boundaries that even experts delineate inconsistently.
We propose Constrained Region Erasing with Soft Targets (CREST) , a Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation (WSSS) framework that generates masks solely from image-level labels.
Our approach builds on Adversarial Erasing (AER) , which iteratively mines discriminative regions, erases them, and retrains a classifier to reveal complementary cues that become pseudo-labels for segmentation.
However, standard AER also collects irrelevant background features, degrading pseudo-label quality. CREST addresses this with (i) a Constrained Ordinal Region Expansion (CORE) module that encodes the spatial-connectedness prior of polar lows, constraining region expansion from a high-confidence seed, and (ii) a Dynamic Bootstrapping (DB) loss that treats the mining order as a proxy for label reliability, attenuating supervision from noisier, later-mined regions.
On Sentinel-1 SAR data, CREST follows the cyclone structure more closely than standard AER , and returns a multi-class rather than binary mask whose classes indicate the reliability assigned to each region.
We further evaluate on BUS-UCLM breast ultrasound and PASCAL VOC person data, whose targets satisfy the same connectedness prior but come with the dense masks the SAR data lacks.
On both datasets, CREST performs better than the equivalent AER pipeline under identical settings.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Polar lows are small but intense maritime cyclones with horizontal scales of approximately 200 200 – 1,000 1{,}000 km and lifetimes typically shorter than a day [ 1 ] . They form at high latitudes over open water, often close to sea ice or snow-covered land. Their formation is driven by atmospheric instability caused by cold air moving over warmer oceans [ 2 ] . Promptly detecting and localizing polar lows is critical, as they pose risks to maritime activities [ 1 ] and, when making landfall, can disrupt land and air traffic, damage infrastructure, and trigger avalanches [ 3 ] . However, polar lows are also difficult to observe because they frequently occur during the polar night, which prevents the use of visible-light sensors. On the other hand, high-resolution Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from European Space Agency (ESA) ’s Sentinel-1 do not depend on sunlight and provide day-and-night coverage, making them well suited to our setting [ 3 ] ( Figure 1 ). The dataset’s positive class comprises maritime mesocyclones, the broader meteorological class to which polar lows belong [ 3 ] . Throughout the paper, “polar low” denotes the positive class in this dataset. (a) Positive (polar low present) (b) Negative (Background) Fig. 1 : Examples of Sentinel-1 SAR imagery from our dataset. (a) A positive sample showing a polar low. (b) A negative sample showing a typical maritime background without cyclonic activity. The black regions are “no-data” areas in the SAR images. In recent years, machine learning has been increasingly adopted to analyze and track cyclones [ 4 ] and polar lows [ 5 ] . Deep learning architectures for computer vision, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) , have been successfully employed to detect polar lows in SAR imagery with high accuracy [ 3 ] . Determining whether a polar low is present is treated as an image classification task [ 3 ] , while producing a spatial mask can be framed as image segmentation, i.e., pixel-wise classification [ 6 ] . In this work, the target mask represents the SAR -visible footprint of the cyclone, i.e., the area where its wind pattern on the sea surface is visible in the image. Such a spatial output is more informative than an image-level prediction. However, training semantic segmentation networks typically requires dense pixel-level annotations from an expert. In contrast, training a classification network only requires image-level labels, which are much faster and cheaper to obtain. In our case study, however, the obstacle is not only cost. The SAR -visible footprint has diffuse and irregular boundaries that experts might delineate inconsistently because there are no broadly accepted definitions of where a polar low ends. Those diffuse boundaries also affect the methods that could be used to automate the annotation procedure, since refinement pipelines and promptable foundation models alike rely on strong intensity edges and clear foreground-background contrast ( Section II ). Our aim is therefore not to compete with such methods on the benchmarks where they excel, but to obtain spatial labels in a setting where they do not apply. This raises the question of whether the pixel-level masks needed for segmentation can be obtained from image-level labels alone. Feature attribution methods provide a possible route: they explain a classifier by assigning importance scores to input regions according to their contribution to a prediction [ 7 , 8 ] . These scores are commonly visualized as saliency maps or heatmaps and, for binary classification, can in principle localize the target object [ 9 , 10 ] . A prominent research direction therefore thresholds and refines such heatmaps into pixel-level masks, which are used either directly as segmentations or as pseudo-labels for training a segmentation model, using only image-level labels and without manual pixel-level annotations [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . However, such heatmaps are typically coarse, and earlier applications to polar low SAR imagery primarily captured a few characteristic cues (e.g., the cyclone eye) while overlooking boundaries and secondary structures [ 3 ] . The limited spatial coverage of a single saliency map motivates an iterative search for less discriminative object regions. Adversarial Erasing (AER) provides such a mechanism and is an established weakly supervised approach for generating pixel-level pseudo-labels from image-level labels [ 14 ] . In its standard formulation, an initial CNN classifier is trained using image-level labels. AER then iteratively “erases” the most discriminative regions identified by saliency maps and retrains the classifier on the modified images. Each iteration forces the CNN to learn new, less salient features, gradually expanding its focus from the most discriminative regions to those with secondary structures. After thresholding and aggregating the saliency maps obtained across iterations, the mined regions can thus be converted into pseudo-labels that provide pixel-level supervision for a segmentation network, which can then operate directly on new images without repeating the iterative erasure process. Original image Grad-CAM activation Fig. 2 : Spurious background activations during late AER iterations. Each row shows a different positive polar low SAR image. Left: original input. Right: Grad-CAM on the image after erasing mined regions. With most of the target regions removed, the classifier starts producing activations on the background, injecting noise into the aggregated pseudo-label. Although vanilla AER extends segmentation beyond the most discriminative regions identified by a single application of a saliency method, it suffers from two main limitations. • Classifiers trained in early iterations capture the most salient parts of the cyclone. Later classifiers may instead focus on spurious background features, especially when few cyclone cues remain, as shown in Figure 2 . This effect is exacerbated when polar lows have different apparent sizes and are therefore erased at different stages, since smaller cyclones are fully removed after a few iterations while larger ones require more. • Standard AER treats all iterations equally, merging all discovered regions into a single binary mask. This mixes reliable early-discovered regions with less reliable ones discovered in later stages. Treating reliable and unreliable patterns identified at different stages equally degrades the quality of supervision offered by the pseudo-labels for training a segmentation network. (a) Input Image (b) Iter 0 (c) Iter 1 (d) Iter 2 (e) Iter 3 (f) Iter 4 Fig. 3 : Impact of CORE on region expansion. The panels display the Grad-CAM saliency maps at each step of the mining process. Once activated, CORE introduces the yellow local envelope that limits subsequent mask growth. In Iteration 3, the classifier produces a strong activation on land outside this envelope; the activation is therefore excluded from the next mask update, as shown in Iteration 4. To address AER ’s limitations, we introduce Constrained Region Erasing with Soft Targets (CREST) , which combines two main contributions. First, we add a new module, called Constrained Ordinal Region Expansion (CORE) , designed to regulate the iterative growth of discovered regions through a spatial proximity constraint. The mechanism implemented by CORE is illustrated in Figure 3 . After activation, CORE excludes newly mined pixels outside a local envelope around the accumulated support, which are the ones that typically correspond to spurious background features. This design fits the polar low setting, where the SAR -visible pattern is typically compact, and its peripheral regions can be found by expanding locally around the initial seeds. Figure 4 (top) summarizes the whole iterative train-extract-erase loop. Fig. 4 : AER+CORE pipeline and pseudo-label construction. Top: the proposed iterative train → \rightarrow extract → \rightarrow erase loop. We retrain the classifier after each erasing step and recompute Grad-CAM on the updated image. Once activated, CORE restricts the next erasure to a neighborhood (yellow envelope) around the previously mined region. Bottom: Grad-CAM heatmaps from successive iterations and the resulting multi-class pseudo-label, where the class records when each region was mined. Second, we train the segmentation network with a Dynamic Bootstrapping (DB) loss that relaxes supervision where the pseudo-labels are least reliable. To expose that reliability, we preserve the iteration in which AER mines each region as a mining-order tier, moving from binary to multi-class pseudo-labels. Figure 4 (bottom) illustrates how heatmaps progressively expand the coverage over iterations to form the final pseudo-label. For early-mined pixels, which are assumed to be more reliable, the loss supervises the network mostly through the pseudo-label. For later-mined pixels, it progressively attenuates cross-entropy supervision from the pseudo-label, reducing the influence of potentially noisy regions. Our main focus is polar low segmentation in Sentinel-1 SAR imagery. Since pixel-level ground-truth masks are unavailable in this domain, we compare the predictions qualitatively against the baselines across test scenes and place the mined tiers in physical context by overlaying the SAR acquisition with the meteorological fields. Then, we evaluate CREST on the UCLM Breast Ultrasound lesion Segmentation (BUS) and PASCAL VOC 2012 datasets. We select both datasets because their targets satisfy the same spatial-connectedness prior that motivates CORE , namely that each object occupies a coherent region whose peripheral parts are reached by expanding locally from an initial seed. Ultrasound lesions form compact, connected masses, and in VOC we restrict the evaluation to the “person” class, whose instances are likewise spatially connected, which also preserves a binary foreground-background setting comparable to the polar low task. Unlike the polar low dataset, these two provide pixel-level masks, which we use only for evaluation and never for training. They let us measure our pipeline against the AER baseline quantitatively, a comparison the polar low data cannot support for lack of dense ground truth.

sections.heading: II-A Deep Learning for Polar Low Detection
sections.text: The detection and analysis of polar lows have traditionally relied on manual inspection of satellite imagery [ 1 ] or on threshold-based rules applied to reanalysis data [ 15 ] . Compared to these traditional procedures, deep learning provides data-driven approaches for automated detection and tracking of polar lows across different data modalities. Early works, such as Krinitskiy et al. [ 16 ] , showed that CNNs can perform binary polar low classification on satellite mosaics. A recent review notes that deep learning has been used to detect maritime polar mesoscale cyclones in satellite imagery, and that SAR observations, despite resolving the atmospheric fronts and cyclonic centers that identify these systems, have so far rarely been exploited for polar lows [ 17 ] . For instance, Zhang et al. [ 18 ] combined SAR and radiometer observations to support automated tracking, which illustrates the value of multi-modal inputs. Visible imagers depend on sunlight, whereas thermal-infrared sensors, passive-microwave radiometers, and microwave scatterometers can provide nighttime observations but generally have coarser spatial resolution than Sentinel-1 SAR . SAR is independent of solar illumination and provides the high spatial resolution useful for examining mesoscale wind patterns. In this context, Grahn and Bianchi [ 3 ] introduced the first publicly available Sentinel-1 SAR dataset for polar low classification and established a baseline using CNNs . Their study indicates that SAR imagery contains enough information to distinguish polar low patterns from other atmospheric phenomena. To interpret the CNN classifier decisions, Grahn and Bianchi used Explainable AI (XAI) methods, including Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) [ 10 ] and Integrated Gradients [ 19 ] , to produce heatmaps that indicate which image regions contribute the most to the predicted class ( Figure 5 ). However, a model trained for image-level classification is not required to account for the target pattern across its full spatial extent. It may instead focus on a few discriminative cues, such as the cyclone eye or strong wind fronts, while neglecting weaker peripheral structures. Consequently, masks obtained from individual saliency maps are often coarse and incomplete, which limits their usefulness as pixel-level supervision. (a) Original SAR image (b) Grad-CAM (c) Integrated Gradients Fig. 5 : Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients on a Sentinel-1 SAR image. In this example, both methods highlight the most discriminative cues but not the full spatial extent of the cyclone.

sections.heading: II-B Weakly Supervised Segmentation and Foundation Models
sections.text: The core objective of Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation (WSSS) is to derive dense segmentation masks from weak supervision, which typically comes in the form of image-level labels. Many established approaches start by thresholding a saliency map and refining it through post-processing. For example, Forest et al. [ 12 ] refine saliency maps using thresholding and morphological closing to fill small gaps and connect nearby activated regions. Other methods combine seed expansion with a boundary-aware constraint, as in the Seed-Expand-Constrain framework [ 20 ] . (a) Sentinel-1 SAR input image. (b) Grid-based prompting highlights satellite imaging artifacts. (c) In this example, box-based prompting misses the diffuse cyclone structure. Fig. 6 : Zero-shot SAM outputs for one Sentinel-1 polar low SAR image. With grid- and box-based prompts, the model highlights imaging artifacts or misses the diffuse cyclone structure. Foundation models like the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [ 21 , 22 ] provide interactive segmentation capabilities on natural images, and recent work explores their use in remote sensing [ 23 ] . However, both classical refinement methods and promptable segmentation models generally rely on clear boundaries and strong foreground-background contrast. This assumption does not hold for SAR imagery of atmospheric phenomena such as polar lows, whose diffuse boundaries fade gradually into the background. In our zero-shot SAM experiment using grid- and box-based prompts, the model responded to high-contrast imaging artifacts (e.g., satellite scan lines) rather than the diffuse cyclone structure ( Figure 6 ). Box- and scribble-supervised methods that use boundary cues to expand sparse labels may face similar challenges in this setting [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] .

sections.heading: II-C Adversarial Erasing
sections.text: AER [ 14 ] methods are specifically designed to address the incomplete localization of classification-based saliency maps. In AER , a classifier is trained to identify discriminative object regions through saliency maps. These regions are then erased from the input images, and the classifier is retrained on the modified dataset. This cycle forces the classifier to discover new, less discriminative features of the object that were previously overshadowed by more salient patterns. By aggregating the saliency maps generated across several iterations, one can obtain more complete object coverage than with a single saliency map. Standard AER pipelines often refine segmentation outputs with Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) [ 14 , 28 , 29 ] . The original AER method also uses Prohibitive Segmentation Learning to weight class contributions [ 14 ] . For polar low SAR imagery, diffuse cyclone boundaries provide weak cues for edge-based refinement, and we therefore omit this stage throughout, as detailed in Section V . In addition, naive aggregation across iterations can inject noise since, when most of the informative regions are erased, the classifier may attend to background texture or imaging artifacts, which produces spurious activations ( Figure 2 ). Thus, there are two key challenges for extending AER -based methods to polar low segmentation: limiting spurious region growth across iterations and reducing the influence of later, potentially noisy discoveries.

sections.heading: IV Methodology
sections.text: In this section, we present CREST , our two-stage pipeline for weakly supervised polar low segmentation in SAR imagery. A single discriminative classifier responds only to the most prominent parts of the target, such as the cyclone eye, which is why the mining procedure is made iterative. Iteration in turn raises two challenges: the discovered region can expand into unrelated background, and regions found in later iterations provide progressively less reliable supervision. To address them, CREST implements a two-stage procedure illustrated in Figure 7 . Stage 1 generates pixel-level pseudo-labels from image-level labels using the proposed AER+CORE, an enhanced AER procedure in which CORE constrains the iterative mining process. Stage 2 trains a dedicated segmentation network using the generated pseudo-labels and a DB strategy to handle their inherent noise and uncertainty. The two stages are detailed below. Fig. 7 : Overview of the proposed two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 generates mining-order pseudo-labels from image-level labels via AER with the CORE module. Stage 2 trains a segmentation network using these pseudo-labels and a Dynamic Bootstrapping strategy to handle label uncertainty.

Unlike a flat binary mask, this representation preserves the mining order, which Stage 2 uses in two ways: as the reliability signal by which it modulates supervision, and as the label space it predicts over, so that the ordering survives into the segmentation output rather than being collapsed at training time.

sections.heading: IV-B Stage 2: Segmentation Network Training
sections.text: Stage 2 trains a shared image-to-mask model on the original images 𝐗 i \mathbf{X}_{i} paired with the Stage 1 pseudo-labels 𝐏 i \mathbf{P}_{i} ; the erased images are used only during Stage 1. Unlike the instance-specific attribution maps, the trained segmentation model can be applied directly to unseen images and can learn spatial patterns shared across the training set rather than reproducing every attribution artifact. This provides a mechanism for reducing noise and fragmentation in the Stage 1 pseudo-labels. Although the pseudo-label tiers are ordered by mining iteration, the “distance” between them is not metric (i.e., class 3 is not “three times” as reliable as class 1). Therefore, we formulate the training task as a pixel-wise classification problem using a cross-entropy loss rather than a regression-based approach. Treating them as categorical classes allows us to assign independent reliability weights to each tier, providing better control over the supervision signal.

sections.heading: V Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we evaluate the proposed CREST pipeline. We first outline our evaluation strategy, which addresses the lack of pixel-level ground truth for the primary SAR images. Then, we describe how we perform the comparative analysis against baselines and discuss the results. We conclude by presenting a progressive ablation study of the proposed modules. We defer to Appendix D the description of the datasets, including those unrelated to our case study, that are used for quantitative benchmarking, while in Appendix E we detail the experimental setup.

sections.heading: V-A Evaluation Strategy
sections.text: Unless otherwise stated, all results reported in this section are computed on the masks predicted by the trained Stage 2 segmentation network, not on the raw pseudo-labels produced by Stage 1. The pseudo-labels are an intermediate supervision signal: they guide optimization of the segmentation model but remain noisy and image-specific by construction. Evaluating the trained segmentation network is therefore the relevant endpoint because it is the deployable component of the pipeline. Since the SAR dataset has no pixel-level ground truth, we assess the predicted masks qualitatively, comparing them against those produced by the baselines on the visible cyclone structure across test scenes. The gallery in Appendix A and a consistency check under geometric transformations in Appendix B show additional results. In addition, we overlay an acquisition with auxiliary Sea Level Pressure (SLP) and 10 m wind fields from ECMWF reanalysis version 5 (ERA5) [ 33 ] to place the mined tiers in physical context. To complement this qualitative analysis with a quantitative evaluation, we also apply the proposed pipeline to two public datasets that provide pixel-level ground truth: BUS [ 34 ] , a dataset of breast ultrasound images for tumor segmentation, and VOC [ 35 ] , a standard computer vision benchmark. In VOC , we select the person class to form a binary semantic segmentation task; an image may contain multiple people as well as objects from other classes. We select these two datasets because their targets are compatible with the same spatial-connectedness prior of CORE , namely that each object forms a coherent region whose peripheral parts can be reached by expanding locally from the most discriminative seed. Each tumor is a compact, connected mass, and person instances are likewise spatially connected. Having multiple instances within the same image does not conflict with this prior: thresholding the accumulated heatmap yields one seed per instance, and because the CORE envelope is a dilation of the entire current mask, each seed expands within its own local neighborhood. The last rows of Figures 11 and 12 show this for two detached lesions and for multiple people. These two datasets therefore serve two purposes. First, they make the results easier to judge, since the boundaries of tumors and persons are less ambiguous than those of a cyclone. Second, they carry the pixel-level ground truth that the SAR dataset does not, which allows CREST and standard AER to be compared numerically under identical settings ( Section V-B ). This comparison is not a claim of benchmark performance: all methods run under a deliberately minimal shared protocol with no post-processing, so the absolute values reported here sit well below what specialized state-of-the-art methods achieve on either dataset. What these tables are for is the difference between CREST and standard AER, measured where the predicted masks can actually be scored, which is what the polar low data do not allow.

sections.heading: V-B Method Comparison
sections.text: We benchmark our proposed pipeline against two baselines to assess the contribution of each component.

sections.heading: Grad-CAM
sections.text: This baseline represents the simplest of the weakly supervised approaches. We generate a single Grad-CAM attribution map from the classifier and threshold it (top 30%) to create a binary pseudo-label, which is used to supervise the segmentation network. This method relies entirely on the initial discriminative regions found by the classifier without performing any iterative discovery of new regions.

sections.heading: Standard AER
sections.text: This is the vanilla adversarial erasing pipeline. It employs an iterative mining strategy: after training the classifier, the most discriminative regions are erased, and the classifier is retrained on the modified images to discover new, complementary features. Once the mining procedure is complete, all regions discovered across iterations are merged into a single binary mask, which serves as the pseudo-label for the segmentation network.

sections.heading: CREST (ours)
sections.text: Our full method builds upon standard AER by integrating two main components: the CORE module constrains new region growth during mining, while the DB loss uses the preserved mining order as a proxy for reliability and attenuates cross-entropy supervision from later-mined regions. To ensure a controlled comparison, all methods use the same Xception backbone, Grad-CAM implementation, SegFormer architecture, and training schedule. The standalone Grad-CAM reference uses a top-30% threshold, whereas the iterative methods use the dataset-specific absolute thresholds reported in Appendix E . Consequently, the standalone Grad-CAM baseline is not identical to iteration 0 of standard AER ; the latter is reported in Appendix C as the single-pass reference under the iterative-method protocol. The original AER formulation builds both its classification and segmentation networks on DeepLab-CRF-LargeFOV, applies a CRF to post-process the segmentation output at test time, and in an optional further round uses CRF -refined training-set predictions as supervision [ 14 , 28 , 29 ] . However, we decided not to apply CRF because it relies on strong intensity edges, which the diffuse cyclone boundaries in SAR imagery do not provide. We, therefore, omitted this stage in the polar low setting and on BUS and VOC as well, holding all methods to identical conditions.

Since quantitative ground truth is unavailable, we rely on visual inspection across test scenes. For the SAR results, the iterative methods retain mining iterations up to t = 4 t=4 , so CREST masks can show up to five foreground tiers, and fewer when the network does not predict all of them in a given image. Figure 9 illustrates the limitations of the Grad-CAM and AER baselines. The Grad-CAM approach (second column) focuses mainly on the cyclone eye in these examples and does not capture the full visible extent of the system. Standard AER (third column) mines larger regions but can also drift into the background and include unrelated wind-driven sea-surface patterns or other background features. In these examples, CREST (fourth column) produces spatially coherent masks that follow spiral- and comma-like structures while avoiding the broad background expansion seen for standard AER . The same behavior holds over the gallery of Appendix A and under the geometric transformations of Appendix B . The tiers also carry information that the binary output of standard AER discards: warm colors mark the regions mined first and cool colors those mined last, so a single prediction records both where the model places the cyclone and in what order it recovered its parts. Figure 10 places one prediction in meteorological context. SLP and 10 m wind are diagnostic variables for mesocyclones, since a mature system is associated with a compact sea-level pressure minimum and with strong, organized near-surface winds that wrap around the vortex and its frontal bands. In this scene, the early-mined regions (yellow/orange) lie near the low-pressure center while later-mined tiers (purple/blue) extend into the surrounding circulation, so the mining order runs from the cyclone core outward. These variables are not provided to the segmentation model as inputs or pixel-level supervision, and the overlay is not used to compute segmentation scores. sections.heading: BUS & VOC
sections.text: Following the qualitative cyclone analysis, we now turn to the BUS and VOC datasets, whose first role is to make the mining order legible. The visual comparisons in Figs. 11 and 12 illustrate how the color-coded mining tiers relate to different parts of the target objects in selected examples. In all three datasets, the first tier lands on the most diagnostic part of the target, and later tiers spread outward from it. On VOC , the face and upper body come first, then the rest of the person; on BUS , the lesion core, then its margin; on SAR , the cyclone eye, then the surrounding bands ( Figures 9 and 10 ). VOC shows this most clearly, since the ordering can be judged without domain expertise, whereas on SAR imagery the same judgment requires a meteorologist. That the same core-to-periphery progression appears on all three targets indicates that the mining order follows how strongly a region signals the target, rather than anything specific to cyclones. The ablations below supply a quantitative counterpart: weighting supervision by that order improves the resulting masks, which would not happen if the order carried no information about reliability. These qualitative examples are shown at t = 4 t=4 on BUS and t = 5 t=5 on VOC , independently of the operating points used for the quantitative results below. Since these datasets provide ground-truth masks, they permit a quantitative assessment under the protocols described in Appendix D . At inference, the predicted tier is s ^ u = arg ⁡ max k ⁡ p u , k \hat{s}_{u}=\arg\max_{k}p_{u,k} at each pixel u u . For evaluation, pixels with s ^ u > 0 \hat{s}_{u}>0 are merged into a single foreground class. For the iterative methods, we vary how many mined tiers are retained in the final mask, and Tables I and II report, for each method, its best test result over the evaluated iterations. For traceability, the retained iteration is the one maximizing Macro IoU over the reported sweep, with ties broken by foreground IoU: on BUS , t = 2 t=2 for standard AER, t = 4 t=4 for AER+CORE, and t = 3 t=3 for CREST ; on VOC , t = 4 t=4 for standard AER and AER+CORE, and t = 6 t=6 for CREST , which ties t = 5 t=5 on Macro IoU. Tables IV and V report the full per-iteration sweeps. True positives, false positives, and false negatives are accumulated over all evaluated test pixels before each class score is computed. Foreground IoU and Dice are the primary metrics; Macro IoU and Macro Dice are secondary summaries computed as the unweighted mean over background and foreground. On BUS , CREST reaches a Macro IoU of 64.8 % 64.8\% , compared with 60.2 % 60.2\% for standard AER and 57.2 % 57.2\% for Grad-CAM . For the foreground lesion class, CREST obtains an IoU of 32.7 % 32.7\% against 24.3 % 24.3\% for standard AER , a gap of 8.4 8.4 points. On VOC the two methods are closer, with CREST ahead by 4.0 4.0 points of foreground IoU on the person class. Since these two peaks occur at different iterations, we also compare both methods at the iteration where standard AER peaks ( t = 2 t=2 on BUS , t = 4 t=4 on VOC ). Even at the baseline’s own best iteration, CREST leads by 2.6 2.6 and 1.7 1.7 points of Macro IoU and by 4.4 4.4 and 3.3 3.3 points of foreground IoU (Tables IV and V ), margins that exceed the run-to-run spread measured below. The gaps then widen over the later iterations, to 9.9 9.9 and 13.9 13.9 points on BUS at t = 4 t=4 and to 3.8 3.8 and 6.5 6.5 points on VOC at t = 6 t=6 . Only the earliest VOC iterations run the other way: at t = 1 t=1 and t = 2 t=2 , where little beyond the most discriminative core has been mined, standard AER is marginally ahead in foreground IoU, by 1.5 1.5 and 0.2 0.2 points. This is consistent with the role of the DB loss, which pays off later, once noisier iterations begin to contribute supervision. Taken together, these numbers show that the constrained, tier-aware pipeline improves on standard AER under identical conditions, so the multi-class output and the region constraint do not compromise mask quality. Refinement-based and promptable methods rely on strong intensity edges, which do not appear in the diffuse cyclone boundaries ( Figure 6 ). To our knowledge, standard AER is therefore one of the most suitable approaches currently applicable to polar lows in SAR imagery. BUS and VOC compare standard AER with CREST , so they let us measure the improvement that we can only see qualitatively on the SAR data ( Figure 9 ).

sections.text: Table II quantifies the gain from each module. Starting from the standard AER baseline, the addition of the CORE module (AER+CORE) improves Macro IoU on both datasets ( + 1.2 +1.2 points on BUS and + 1.1 +1.1 points on VOC ), and foreground IoU by + 2.1 +2.1 points on both. sections.heading: Iteration-wise stability
sections.text: Fig. 13 : Macro IoU over retained adversarial-erasing iterations on the BUS test set. Standard AER degrades after iteration 2, whereas the AER+CORE and full CREST (AER+CORE+DB) trajectories vary less over the later iterations. One weakness of standard AER is its sensitivity to the number of retained mining iterations. With few iterations, the pseudo-label may contain only the most discriminative core, leading to under-segmentation. With many iterations, the classifier may increasingly rely on background textures or acquisition artifacts after informative regions have been erased; recall can increase while precision decreases. This behavior is clearly visible in the detailed BUS results in Table IV : standard AER moves from 70.6 % 70.6\% precision / 2.0 % 2.0\% recall at iteration 0 to 19.4 % 19.4\% precision / 53.3 % 53.3\% recall at iteration 4, illustrating the shift from severe under-segmentation to over-expansion. To illustrate this sensitivity, Figure 13 plots final segmentation performance on BUS , indexed by the last retained mining iteration. The curve for vanilla AER (orange) reveals a sharp performance degradation after iteration 2, a pattern consistent with progressively noisier pseudo-label expansion. The CORE trajectory (blue) is flatter over the evaluated later iterations. At the last evaluated iteration on BUS ( t = 4 t=4 , by which point CORE has been active for three iterations), AER+CORE reaches 61.4 % 61.4\% Macro IoU and 26.4 % 26.4\% foreground IoU against 53.4 % 53.4\% and 16.6 % 16.6\% for standard AER (Table IV ), gaps of 8.0 8.0 and 9.8 9.8 points that lie far outside the spread estimated at the start of this subsection. The corresponding gaps on VOC at t = 6 t=6 are smaller, 1.9 1.9 and 3.2 3.2 points, so the effect is most pronounced on the dataset whose baseline degrades most sharply. The full CREST trajectory (green; AER+CORE+DB) also varies less than standard AER over the later iterations. This behavior is consistent with the lower weights assigned to late-mined pixels and indicates reduced, rather than eliminated, sensitivity to the retained-iteration endpoint.

sections.heading: Sensitivity to the attribution method
sections.text: We conclude with a sensitivity check in which the attribution mechanism is changed from Grad-CAM to Grad-CAM++ [ 36 ] , without changing the thresholds or κ \kappa . Table III reports higher values for CREST than for standard AER on both datasets. On BUS , foreground IoU is lower for both methods than with Grad-CAM ( − 5.7 -5.7 and − 10.0 -10.0 points), possibly because the fixed thresholds and κ \kappa are less well suited to the activation profile of Grad-CAM++, whereas on VOC both methods improve slightly ( + 0.9 +0.9 and + 1.3 +1.3 points). Under this substitution, the gap in foreground IoU between CREST and standard AER on BUS is 4.1 4.1 points. This suggests that the observed advantage over standard AER is retained when the attribution method is changed.

sections.heading: VI Conclusions
sections.text: In this work, we presented CREST , a novel weakly supervised framework for training a neural network for image segmentation. We designed the proposed method to bridge the gap between binary classification labels and pixel-level understanding of polar lows in SAR imagery. While standard AER techniques can iteratively discover object features, their mining process can drift into the background and blend irrelevant regions with meaningful target features. We addressed this limitation with two main contributions. First, the CORE module restricts new discoveries to a local envelope around the accumulated support. Second, the tier-aware DB loss uses the preserved mining order as a proxy for reliability and progressively attenuates cross-entropy supervision from later-mined regions. In the qualitative examples, CREST produces visually coherent masks that follow the visible cyclone structure more closely than standard AER , and whose tiers order the mask from the cyclone core outward, with no human delineation entering the pipeline at any stage. On the BUS medical dataset and the VOC benchmark, which unlike the SAR data provide dense masks, the same core-to-periphery ordering appears on targets whose extent is easier to judge than a cyclone’s. At each method’s best iteration, CREST improves on standard AER by 8.4 8.4 points of foreground IoU on BUS and 4.0 4.0 points on VOC ; compared at the iteration where the baseline itself peaks, the margins are 4.4 4.4 and 3.3 3.3 points, and they widen over the later iterations. Since refinement-based methods do not apply to diffuse cyclone boundaries, standard AER is, to our knowledge, the best approach currently applicable to polar lows, so these margins measure the improvement that the SAR data can only show qualitatively. These experiments validate the mechanism under dense ground truth rather than compete on these benchmarks: no CRF or other post-processing is applied to any method, so the absolute values remain below what specialized state-of-the-art segmentation methods achieve on either dataset. The current formulation of CORE assumes locally coherent growth around the already discovered support. Although this constraint could be relaxed in future work, the results show that CREST can extract spatial structure from image-level labels in different settings. From a meteorological perspective, this is an important practical contribution because dense cyclone masks are scarce and difficult to standardize: their boundaries are diffuse, evolve rapidly, and often require expert interpretation. Our framework provides a scalable route for generating candidate spatial labels from existing detection archives. The masks could support future studies of cyclone size, shape, compactness, asymmetry, and internal structure, as well as their relationship with surrounding environmental fields. More broadly, the same weakly supervised paradigm is relevant to other meteorological events for which pixel-level masks are scarce and difficult to obtain because the phenomena have fuzzy boundaries and require expert interpretation. In this context, CREST can help generate spatial labels in scientific domains where they are currently missing.

sections.heading: Appendix A Additional Qualitative Results on Polar Lows
sections.text: To provide a broader qualitative view, we present a gallery of segmentation results in Figure 15 . sections.heading: Appendix D Dataset Details
sections.text: In the following, we describe the primary polar low dataset and the two benchmark datasets for quantitative evaluation.

sections.heading: D-A Sentinel-1 Dataset
sections.text: We use the public polar low dataset introduced by Grahn and Bianchi [ 3 ] 1 1 1 https://doi.org/10.18710/FV5T9U . The images are not native optical images, but standardized three-channel composites derived from Sentinel-1 SAR acquisitions. Each sample consists of a standardized SAR -derived RGB composite paired with an image-level binary label, indicating the presence or absence of a cyclone pattern. The dataset provides image-level labels but no pixel-level masks, motivating the weakly supervised setting. The dataset contains 1,982 geocoded samples, of which 318 belong to the positive class and 1,664 to the negative class. The images cover approximately 400 × 400 400\times 400 km at 500 m spacing, corresponding to roughly 800 × 800 800\times 800 pixels. The negative samples are chosen to remain visually challenging, so that background structures and acquisition conditions are comparable to those of the positive cases. Full details on dataset construction, SAR preprocessing, geocoding, and RGB-composite generation are deferred to the original dataset paper [ 3 ] . Pixels outside the valid SAR swath are encoded as zero in the supplied composites and are treated as background during pseudo-label generation and segmentation training. The auxiliary SLP and 10 m wind fields used for the illustrative overlay in Figure 10 are taken from ERA5 [ 33 ] , retrieved as hourly data on single levels from the Copernicus Climate Data Store [ 37 , 38 ] . The Sentinel-1 scene displayed in that figure is the same acquisition as the corresponding dataset sample, retrieved through the Copernicus Browser [ 39 ] for visualization only. These fields are used solely for post-hoc interpretation and are never provided to the model as inputs or supervision. The data are split into 1,547 images used for training—254 positive ( c = 1 c=1 ) and 1,293 negative ( c = 0 c=0 )—and 435 images for testing—64 positive ( c = 1 c=1 ) and 371 negative ( c = 0 c=0 ). Since the dataset lacks an official validation split, we use a stratified 80/20 split of the training set for model selection.

sections.heading: D-B BUS
sections.text: We use a dataset of breast ultrasound images containing pixel-level masks for three classes: benign tumors, malignant tumors, and normal tissue (no lesion). We merge benign and malignant tumors into the positive class ( c = 1 c=1 ) and use normal tissue as the negative class ( c = 0 c=0 ). Totals: 419 negative, 264 positive. Some images contain clinician overlays (bounding boxes, text) that could act as shortcuts for the classifier. We identify these artifacts and replace them with interpolated values to ensure a fair learning process. We form the training, validation, and test subsets using stratified group splitting by patient, reserving approximately 20% of the data for testing. All images from a patient remain in the same subset, so the splits are patient-disjoint.

sections.heading: D-C VOC (person-only, binarized)
sections.text: We use a custom subset derived from PASCAL VOC 2012, treating all person instances as foreground ( c = 1 c=1 ) and other labeled classes as background ( c = 0 c=0 ). The recorded split contains 1,595 positive and 1,595 negative development images, and 399 positive and 399 negative held-out images. A validation subset is obtained through a stratified 80/20 split of the development set.

sections.heading: Appendix E Experimental Settings
sections.text: In the following, we describe the experimental setting used for the two stages. All experiments are performed on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB). All quantitative results are reported from a single run initialized with seed s = 42 s=42 .

sections.heading: Stage 1—Pseudo-label generation
sections.text: The classifier uses an Xception [ 40 ] backbone pretrained on ImageNet-1K [ 41 , 42 ] , followed by global average pooling and a multi-layer perceptron configured with 2048 → 32 → 2 2048\to 32\to 2 neurons. The classifier is optimized using Adam [ 43 ] ( lr = 5 × 10 − 4 \mathrm{lr}=5\times 10^{-4} ) and CE . The binarization thresholds for the Grad-CAM heatmaps are 0.7 (cyclone), 0.85 ( VOC ), and 0.9 ( BUS ). In the zero-based indexing of Algorithm 1 , CORE uses t core = 3 t_{\mathrm{core}}=3 and κ = 0.3 \kappa=0.3 for cyclone/ VOC , and t core = 2 t_{\mathrm{core}}=2 and κ = 0.15 \kappa=0.15 for BUS . The number of iterations N N in the AER +CORE loop is 7 for cyclone and VOC , and 5 for BUS . We use early stopping and the ReduceLROnPlateau callback (factor 0.5, patience 7), monitoring the validation loss. Augmentations include translation/rotation/scale, flips, and random erasing [ 44 ] . Color jitter is added for BUS . Inputs are resized to 512 × 512 512\times 512 for cyclone/ BUS and to 480 × 480 480\times 480 for VOC .

sections.heading: Stage 2—Segmentation training
sections.text: We initialize SegFormer [ 45 ] from a MiT-B3 checkpoint pretrained on ImageNet-1K [ 41 , 42 ] and then densely supervised on ADE20K [ 46 ] . We train SegFormer on pseudo-labels using AdamW [ 47 ] ( lr = 5 × 10 − 4 \mathrm{lr}=5\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 0.02), batch size 16. We use early stopping and ReduceLROnPlateau (factor 0.5, patience 7), monitoring validation F1 against the Stage 1 pseudo-labels, so that no dense annotation enters Stage 2 training on any dataset. Dense masks exist only for BUS and VOC , where they are used after training to compute the reported metrics. As the loss, we use Dice+ CE with DB (equal CE /Dice weighting, α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 ; tier reliabilities ρ s \rho_{s} : [0.8, 0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0] for cyclone/ VOC , [0.8, 0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0] for BUS ). Augmentations and input resizing are the same as in Stage 1. One full run of a given configuration therefore comprises the N N Stage 1 classifier cycles described above and a single Stage 2 training run. No CRF or other post-processing is applied at either stage, for any method, on any of the three datasets.

Grahn and F. M. Bianchi are with NORCE, The Norwegian Research Centre AS Abstract Polar lows are intense maritime cyclones that form rapidly at high latitudes. Deep learning can detect them in Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, but pixel-level segmentation remains an open challenge. No pixel-level masks are available for training, and a polar low’s extent is inherently subjective, with diffuse boundaries that even experts delineate inconsistently. We propose Constrained Region Erasing with Soft Targets (CREST) , a Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation (WSSS) framework that generates masks solely from image-level labels. Our approach builds on Adversarial Erasing (AER) , which iteratively mines discriminative regions, erases them, and retrains a classifier to reveal complementary cues that become pseudo-labels for segmentation. However, standard AER also collects irrelevant background features, degrading pseudo-label quality. CREST addresses this with (i) a Constrained Ordinal Region Expansion (CORE) module that encodes the spatial-connectedness prior of polar lows, constraining region expansion from a high-confidence seed, and (ii) a Dynamic Bootstrapping (DB) loss that treats the mining order as a proxy for label reliability, attenuating supervision from noisier, later-mined regions. On Sentinel-1 SAR data, CREST follows the cyclone structure more closely than standard AER , and returns a multi-class rather than binary mask whose classes indicate the reliability assigned to each region. We further evaluate on BUS-UCLM breast ultrasound and PASCAL VOC person data, whose targets satisfy the same connectedness prior but come with the dense masks the SAR data lacks. On both datasets, CREST performs better than the equivalent AER pipeline under identical settings. Index Terms: Weakly Supervised Segmentation; Polar Lows; SAR; Adversarial Erasing I Introduction Polar lows are small but intense maritime cyclones with horizontal scales of approximately 200 200 – 1,000 1{,}000 km and lifetimes typically shorter than a day [ 1 ] . They form at high latitudes over open water, often close to sea ice or snow-covered land. Their formation is driven by atmospheric instability caused by cold air moving over warmer oceans [ 2 ] . Promptly detecting and localizing polar lows is critical, as they pose risks to maritime activities [ 1 ] and, when making landfall, can disrupt land and air traffic, damage infrastructure, and trigger avalanches [ 3 ] . However, polar lows are also difficult to observe because they frequently occur during the polar night, which prevents the use of visible-light sensors. On the other hand, high-resolution Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from European Space Agency (ESA) ’s Sentinel-1 do not depend on sunlight and provide day-and-night coverage, making them well suited to our setting [ 3 ] ( Figure 1 ). The dataset’s positive class comprises maritime mesocyclones, the broader meteorological class to which polar lows belong [ 3 ] . Throughout the paper, “polar low” denotes the positive class in this dataset. (a) Positive (polar low present) (b) Negative (Background) Fig. 1 : Examples of Sentinel-1 SAR imagery from our dataset. (a) A positive sample showing a polar low. (b) A negative sample showing a typical maritime background without cyclonic activity. The black regions are “no-data” areas in the SAR images. In recent years, machine learning has been increasingly adopted to analyze and track cyclones [ 4 ] and polar lows [ 5 ] . Deep learning architectures for computer vision, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) , have been successfully employed to detect polar lows in SAR imagery with high accuracy [ 3 ] . Determining whether a polar low is present is treated as an image classification task [ 3 ] , while producing a spatial mask can be framed as image segmentation, i.e., pixel-wise classification [ 6 ] . In this work, the target mask represents the SAR -visible footprint of the cyclone, i.e., the area where its wind pattern on the sea surface is visible in the image. Such a spatial output is more informative than an image-level prediction. However, training semantic segmentation networks typically requires dense pixel-level annotations from an expert. In contrast, training a classification network only requires image-level labels, which are much faster and cheaper to obtain. In our case study, however, the obstacle is not only cost. The SAR -visible footprint has diffuse and irregular boundaries that experts might delineate inconsistently because there are no broadly accepted definitions of where a polar low ends. Those diffuse boundaries also affect the methods that could be used to automate the annotation procedure, since refinement pipelines and promptable foundation models alike rely on strong intensity edges and clear foreground-background contrast ( Section II ). Our aim is therefore not to compete with such methods on the benchmarks where they excel, but to obtain spatial labels in a setting where they do not apply. This raises the question of whether the pixel-level masks needed for segmentation can be obtained from image-level labels alone. Feature attribution methods provide a possible route: they explain a classifier by assigning importance scores to input regions according to their contribution to a prediction [ 7 , 8 ] . These scores are commonly visualized as saliency maps or heatmaps and, for binary classification, can in principle localize the target object [ 9 , 10 ] . A prominent research direction therefore thresholds and refines such heatmaps into pixel-level masks, which are used either directly as segmentations or as pseudo-labels for training a segmentation model, using only image-level labels and without manual pixel-level annotations [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . However, such heatmaps are typically coarse, and earlier applications to polar low SAR imagery primarily captured a few characteristic cues (e.g., the cyclone eye) while overlooking boundaries and secondary structures [ 3 ] . The limited spatial coverage of a single saliency map motivates an iterative search for less discriminative object regions. Adversarial Erasing (AER) provides such a mechanism and is an established weakly supervised approach for generating pixel-level pseudo-labels from image-level labels [ 14 ] . In its standard formulation, an initial CNN classifier is trained using image-level labels. AER then iteratively “erases” the most discriminative regions identified by saliency maps and retrains the classifier on the modified images. Each iteration forces the CNN to learn new, less salient features, gradually expanding its focus from the most discriminative regions to those with secondary structures. After thresholding and aggregating the saliency maps obtained across iterations, the mined regions can thus be converted into pseudo-labels that provide pixel-level supervision for a segmentation network, which can then operate directly on new images without repeating the iterative erasure process. Original image Grad-CAM activation Fig. 2 : Spurious background activations during late AER iterations. Each row shows a different positive polar low SAR image. Left: original input. Right: Grad-CAM on the image after erasing mined regions. With most of the target regions removed, the classifier starts producing activations on the background, injecting noise into the aggregated pseudo-label. Although vanilla AER extends segmentation beyond the most discriminative regions identified by a single application of a saliency method, it suffers from two main limitations. • Classifiers trained in early iterations capture the most salient parts of the cyclone. Later classifiers may instead focus on spurious background features, especially when few cyclone cues remain, as shown in Figure 2 . This effect is exacerbated when polar lows have different apparent sizes and are therefore erased at different stages, since smaller cyclones are fully removed after a few iterations while larger ones require more. • Standard AER treats all iterations equally, merging all discovered regions into a single binary mask. This mixes reliable early-discovered regions with less reliable ones discovered in later stages. Treating reliable and unreliable patterns identified at different stages equally degrades the quality of supervision offered by the pseudo-labels for training a segmentation network. Once activated, CORE introduces the yellow local envelope that limits subsequent mask growth. In Iteration 3, the classifier produces a strong activation on land outside this envelope; the activation is therefore excluded from the next mask update, as shown in Iteration 4. To address AER ’s limitations, we introduce Constrained Region Erasing with Soft Targets (CREST) , which combines two main contributions. First, we add a new module, called Constrained Ordinal Region Expansion (CORE) , designed to regulate the iterative growth of discovered regions through a spatial proximity constraint. The mechanism implemented by CORE is illustrated in Figure 3 . After activation, CORE excludes newly mined pixels outside a local envelope around the accumulated support, which are the ones that typically correspond to spurious background features. This design fits the polar low setting, where the SAR -visible pattern is typically compact, and its peripheral regions can be found by expanding locally around the initial seeds. Figure 4 (top) summarizes the whole iterative train-extract-erase loop. Fig. 4 : AER+CORE pipeline and pseudo-label construction. Top: the proposed iterative train → \rightarrow extract → \rightarrow erase loop. We retrain the classifier after each erasing step and recompute Grad-CAM on the updated image. Once activated, CORE restricts the next erasure to a neighborhood (yellow envelope) around the previously mined region. Bottom: Grad-CAM heatmaps from successive iterations and the resulting multi-class pseudo-label, where the class records when each region was mined. Second, we train the segmentation network with a Dynamic Bootstrapping (DB) loss that relaxes supervision where the pseudo-labels are least reliable. To expose that reliability, we preserve the iteration in which AER mines each region as a mining-order tier, moving from binary to multi-class pseudo-labels. Figure 4 (bottom) illustrates how heatmaps progressively expand the coverage over iterations to form the final pseudo-label. For early-mined pixels, which are assumed to be more reliable, the loss supervises the network mostly through the pseudo-label. For later-mined pixels, it progressively attenuates cross-entropy supervision from the pseudo-label, reducing the influence of potentially noisy regions. Our main focus is polar low segmentation in Sentinel-1 SAR imagery. Since pixel-level ground-truth masks are unavailable in this domain, we compare the predictions qualitatively against the baselines across test scenes and place the mined tiers in physical context by overlaying the SAR acquisition with the meteorological fields. Then, we evaluate CREST on the UCLM Breast Ultrasound lesion Segmentation (BUS) and PASCAL VOC 2012 datasets. We select both datasets because their targets satisfy the same spatial-connectedness prior that motivates CORE , namely that each object occupies a coherent region whose peripheral parts are reached by expanding locally from an initial seed. Ultrasound lesions form compact, connected masses, and in VOC we restrict the evaluation to the “person” class, whose instances are likewise spatially connected, which also preserves a binary foreground-background setting comparable to the polar low task. Unlike the polar low dataset, these two provide pixel-level masks, which we use only for evaluation and never for training. They let us measure our pipeline against the AER baseline quantitatively, a comparison the polar low data cannot support for lack of dense ground truth. II Background and Related Work II-A Deep Learning for Polar Low Detection The detection and analysis of polar lows have traditionally relied on manual inspection of satellite imagery [ 1 ] or on threshold-based rules applied to reanalysis data [ 15 ] . Compared to these traditional procedures, deep learning provides data-driven approaches for automated detection and tracking of polar lows across different data modalities. Early works, such as Krinitskiy et al. [ 16 ] , showed that CNNs can perform binary polar low classification on satellite mosaics. A recent review notes that deep learning has been used to detect maritime polar mesoscale cyclones in satellite imagery, and that SAR observations, despite resolving the atmospheric fronts and cyclonic centers that identify these systems, have so far rarely been exploited for polar lows [ 17 ] . For instance, Zhang et al. [ 18 ] combined SAR and radiometer observations to support automated tracking, which illustrates the value of multi-modal inputs. Visible imagers depend on sunlight, whereas thermal-infrared sensors, passive-microwave radiometers, and microwave scatterometers can provide nighttime observations but generally have coarser spatial resolution than Sentinel-1 SAR . SAR is independent of solar illumination and provides the high spatial resolution useful for examining mesoscale wind patterns. In this context, Grahn and Bianchi [ 3 ] introduced the first publicly available Sentinel-1 SAR dataset for polar low classification and established a baseline using CNNs . Their study indicates that SAR imagery contains enough information to distinguish polar low patterns from other atmospheric phenomena. To interpret the CNN classifier decisions, Grahn and Bianchi used Explainable AI (XAI) methods, including Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) [ 10 ] and Integrated Gradients [ 19 ] , to produce heatmaps that indicate which image regions contribute the most to the predicted class ( Figure 5 ). However, a model trained for image-level classification is not required to account for the target pattern across its full spatial extent. It may instead focus on a few discriminative cues, such as the cyclone eye or strong wind fronts, while neglecting weaker peripheral structures. Consequently, masks obtained from individual saliency maps are often coarse and incomplete, which limits their usefulness as pixel-level supervision. (a) Original SAR image (b) Grad-CAM (c) Integrated Gradients Fig. 5 : Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients on a Sentinel-1 SAR image. In this example, both methods highlight the most discriminative cues but not the full spatial extent of the cyclone. II-B Weakly Supervised Segmentation and Foundation Models The core objective of Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation (WSSS) is to derive dense segmentation masks from weak supervision, which typically comes in the form of image-level labels. Many established approaches start by thresholding a saliency map and refining it through post-processing. For example, Forest et al. [ 12 ] refine saliency maps using thresholding and morphological closing to fill small gaps and connect nearby activated regions. Other methods combine seed expansion with a boundary-aware constraint, as in the Seed-Expand-Constrain framework [ 20 ] . (a) Sentinel-1 SAR input image. (b) Grid-based prompting highlights satellite imaging artifacts. (c) In this example, box-based prompting misses the diffuse cyclone structure. Fig. 6 : Zero-shot SAM outputs for one Sentinel-1 polar low SAR image. With grid- and box-based prompts, the model highlights imaging artifacts or misses the diffuse cyclone structure. Foundation models like the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [ 21 , 22 ] provide interactive segmentation capabilities on natural images, and recent work explores their use in remote sensing [ 23 ] . However, both classical refinement methods and promptable segmentation models generally rely on clear boundaries and strong foreground-background contrast. This assumption does not hold for SAR imagery of atmospheric phenomena such as polar lows, whose diffuse boundaries fade gradually into the background. In our zero-shot SAM experiment using grid- and box-based prompts, the model responded to high-contrast imaging artifacts (e.g., satellite scan lines) rather than the diffuse cyclone structure ( Figure 6 ). Box- and scribble-supervised methods that use boundary cues to expand sparse labels may face similar challenges in this setting [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . II-C Adversarial Erasing AER [ 14 ] methods are specifically designed to address the incomplete localization of classification-based saliency maps. In AER , a classifier is trained to identify discriminative object regions through saliency maps. These regions are then erased from the input images, and the classifier is retrained on the modified dataset. This cycle forces the classifier to discover new, less discriminative features of the object that were previously overshadowed by more salient patterns. By aggregating the saliency maps generated across several iterations, one can obtain more complete object coverage than with a single saliency map. Standard AER pipelines often refine segmentation outputs with Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) [ 14 , 28 , 29 ] . The original AER method also uses Prohibitive Segmentation Learning to weight class contributions [ 14 ] . For polar low SAR imagery, diffuse cyclone boundaries provide weak cues for edge-based refinement, and we therefore omit this stage throughout, as detailed in Section V . In addition, naive aggregation across iterations can inject noise since, when most of the informative regions are erased, the classifier may attend to background texture or imaging artifacts, which produces spurious activations ( Figure 2 ). Thus, there are two key challenges for extending AER -based methods to polar low segmentation: limiting spurious region growth across iterations and reducing the influence of later, potentially noisy discoveries. III Problem Formulation We consider the following dataset of image-label pairs: 𝒟 = { ( 𝐗 i , c i ) ∣ 𝐗 i ∈ ℝ W × H × 3 , c i ∈ { 0 , 1 } , i = 1 , … , | 𝒟 | } , \mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{X}_{i},c_{i})\ \mid\ \mathbf{X}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times H\times 3},\ c_{i}\in\{0,1\},\ i=1,\ldots,\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert\}, where each 𝐗 i \mathbf{X}_{i} is an RGB image of width W W and height H H . Although the source SAR images have only two channels, we use the RGB composites provided with the dataset, which were generated following the preprocessing procedure described in [ 3 ] (see Appendix D for details about the dataset). The image-level label c i c_{i} indicates the presence ( c i = 1 c_{i}=1 ) or absence ( c i = 0 c_{i}=0 ) of a polar low. In the following, we refer to images containing a polar low as positive , and those without as negative . For a positive image, the region to be segmented is the area where the cyclone’s sea-surface wind pattern is visible in the SAR image. Let N N be the maximum number of iterations in the AER procedure. The goal is to use only the image-level labels in 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , without any pixel-level annotation, to train a segmentation model f θ : ℝ W × H × 3 → { 0 , … , N } W × H f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{W\times H\times 3}\rightarrow\{0,\ldots,N\}^{W\times H} that maps each input image 𝐗 i \mathbf{X}_{i} to a mining-order map 𝐒 i = f θ ​ ( 𝐗 i ) \mathbf{S}_{i}=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{X}_{i}) , where class 0 denotes background, and classes from 1 to N N record when foreground pixels were mined, with larger values indicating earlier discovery. IV Methodology In this section, we present CREST , our two-stage pipeline for weakly supervised polar low segmentation in SAR imagery. A single discriminative classifier responds only to the most prominent parts of the target, such as the cyclone eye, which is why the mining procedure is made iterative. Iteration in turn raises two challenges: the discovered region can expand into unrelated background, and regions found in later iterations provide progressively less reliable supervision. To address them, CREST implements a two-stage procedure illustrated in Figure 7 . Stage 1 generates pixel-level pseudo-labels from image-level labels using the proposed AER+CORE, an enhanced AER procedure in which CORE constrains the iterative mining process. Stage 2 trains a dedicated segmentation network using the generated pseudo-labels and a DB strategy to handle their inherent noise and uncertainty. The two stages are detailed below. Fig. 7 : Overview of the proposed two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 generates mining-order pseudo-labels from image-level labels via AER with the CORE module. Stage 2 trains a segmentation network using these pseudo-labels and a Dynamic Bootstrapping strategy to handle label uncertainty. IV-A Stage 1: Pseudo-Label Generation This stage transforms weak image-level annotations into dense pixel-level mining-order pseudo-labels. We perform N N mining iterations in a train-extract-erase loop: each iteration trains a classifier and extracts a mask, while an erasing step prepares the data for the next iteration. The iteration at which each pixel is mined determines its mining-order tier. Class 0 0 denotes background, while foreground tiers 1 , … , N 1,\dots,N correspond to regions mined at different iterations; higher tier values indicate earlier discoveries, to which we assign greater reliability. Although the pseudo-label tiers are ordered by mining iteration, the “distance” between them is not metric (i.e., class 3 is not “three times” as reliable as class 1). Therefore, we formulate the training task as a pixel-wise classification problem using a cross-entropy loss rather than a regression-based approach. Treating them as categorical classes allows us to assign independent reliability weights to each tier, providing better control over the supervision signal.
